stir and cries of them. A minute passed. Their voices seemed to rise to
a higher pitch of excitement, and their movements grew faster. Yet none
came within reach. I stood glaring at the blackness. Then suddenly came
hope. What if the Morlocks were afraid? And close on the heels of that
came a strange thing. The darkness seemed to grow luminous. Very dimly
I began to see the Morlocks about me—three battered at my feet—and then
I recognised, with incredulous surprise, that the others were running,
in an incessant stream, as it seemed, from behind me, and away through
the wood in front. And their backs seemed no longer white, but reddish.
As I stood agape, I saw a little red spark go drifting across a gap of
starlight between the branches, and vanish. And at that I understood
the smell of burning wood, the slumbrous murmur that was growing now
into a gusty roar, the red glow, and the Morlocks’ flight.

“Stepping out from behind my tree and looking back, I saw, through the
black pillars of the nearer trees, the flames of the burning forest. It
was my first fire coming after me. With that I looked for Weena, but
she was gone. The hissing and crackling behind me, the explosive thud
as each fresh tree burst into flame, left little time for reflection.
My iron bar still gripped, I followed in the Morlocks’ path. It was a
close race. Once the flames crept forward so swiftly on my right as I
ran that I was outflanked and had to strike off to the left. But at
last I emerged upon a small open space, and as I did so, a Morlock came
blundering towards me, and past me, and went on straight into the fire!
passages.gist: The Traveller's hopeless stand against the Morlocks turns when he realizes his earlier campfire has become a raging forest fire that routs the Morlocks, loses him Weena, and forces his own flight through the flames.

passages.text:
“And now I was to see the most weird and horrible thing, I think, of
all that I beheld in that future age. This whole space was as bright as
day with the reflection of the fire. In the centre was a hillock or
tumulus, surmounted by a scorched hawthorn. Beyond this was another arm
of the burning forest, with yellow tongues already writhing from it,
completely encircling the space with a fence of fire. Upon the hillside
were some thirty or forty Morlocks, dazzled by the light and heat, and
blundering hither and thither against each other in their bewilderment.
At first I did not realise their blindness, and struck furiously at
them with my bar, in a frenzy of fear, as they approached me, killing
one and crippling several more. But when I had watched the gestures of
one of them groping under the hawthorn against the red sky, and heard
their moans, I was assured of their absolute helplessness and misery in
the glare, and I struck no more of them.

“Yet every now and then one would come straight towards me, setting
loose a quivering horror that made me quick to elude him. At one time
the flames died down somewhat, and I feared the foul creatures would
presently be able to see me. I was thinking of beginning the fight by
killing some of them before this should happen; but the fire burst out
again brightly, and I stayed my hand. I walked about the hill among
them and avoided them, looking for some trace of Weena. But Weena was
gone.

“At last I sat down on the summit of the hillock, and watched this
strange incredible company of blind things groping to and fro, and
making uncanny noises to each other, as the glare of the fire beat on
them. The coiling uprush of smoke streamed across the sky, and through
the rare tatters of that red canopy, remote as though they belonged to
another universe, shone the little stars. Two or three Morlocks came
blundering into me, and I drove them off with blows of my fists,
trembling as I did so.
passages.gist: The Traveller finds himself in a fire-encircled clearing watching dazzled Morlocks grope helplessly, attacks them in fear then spares them, and discovers Weena is gone.

passages.text:
“For the most part of that night I was persuaded it was a nightmare. I
bit myself and screamed in a passionate desire to awake. I beat the
ground with my hands, and got up and sat down again, and wandered here
and there, and again sat down. Then I would fall to rubbing my eyes and
calling upon God to let me awake. Thrice I saw Morlocks put their heads
down in a kind of agony and rush into the flames. But, at last, above
the subsiding red of the fire, above the streaming masses of black
smoke and the whitening and blackening tree stumps, and the diminishing
numbers of these dim creatures, came the white light of the day.

“I searched again for traces of Weena, but there were none. It was
plain that they had left her poor little body in the forest. I cannot
describe how it relieved me to think that it had escaped the awful fate
to which it seemed destined. As I thought of that, I was almost moved
to begin a massacre of the helpless abominations about me, but I
contained myself. The hillock, as I have said, was a kind of island in
the forest. From its summit I could now make out through a haze of
smoke the Palace of Green Porcelain, and from that I could get my
bearings for the White Sphinx. And so, leaving the remnant of these
damned souls still going hither and thither and moaning, as the day
grew clearer, I tied some grass about my feet and limped on across
smoking ashes and among black stems that still pulsated internally with
fire, towards the hiding-place of the Time Machine. I walked slowly,
for I was almost exhausted, as well as lame, and I felt the intensest
wretchedness for the horrible death of little Weena. It seemed an
overwhelming calamity. Now, in this old familiar room, it is more like
the sorrow of a dream than an actual loss. But that morning it left me
absolutely lonely again—terribly alone. I began to think of this house
of mine, of this fireside, of some of you, and with such thoughts came
a longing that was pain.
passages.gist: The Traveller endures the burning night in disbelieving anguish, accepts Weena's disappearance with mingled relief and grief at dawn, and limps toward the Time Machine overwhelmed by loneliness and homesickness.

passages.text:
“But, as I walked over the smoking ashes under the bright morning sky,
I made a discovery. In my trouser pocket were still some loose matches.
The box must have leaked before it was lost.

“About eight or nine in the morning I came to the same seat of yellow
metal from which I had viewed the world upon the evening of my arrival.
I thought of my hasty conclusions upon that evening and could not
refrain from laughing bitterly at my confidence. Here was the same
beautiful scene, the same abundant foliage, the same splendid palaces
and magnificent ruins, the same silver river running between its
fertile banks. The gay robes of the beautiful people moved hither and
thither among the trees. Some were bathing in exactly the place where I
had saved Weena, and that suddenly gave me a keen stab of pain. And
like blots upon the landscape rose the cupolas above the ways to the
Underworld. I understood now what all the beauty of the Overworld
people covered. Very pleasant was their day, as pleasant as the day of
the cattle in the field. Like the cattle, they knew of no enemies and
provided against no needs. And their end was the same.

“I grieved to think how brief the dream of the human intellect had
been. It had committed suicide. It had set itself steadfastly towards
comfort and ease, a balanced society with security and permanency as
its watchword, it had attained its hopes—to come to this at last. Once,
life and property must have reached almost absolute safety. The rich
had been assured of his wealth and comfort, the toiler assured of his
life and work. No doubt in that perfect world there had been no
unemployed problem, no social question left unsolved. And a great quiet
had followed.
passages.gist: Returning to his first overlook with leftover matches, the Traveller recognizes the Eloi's beauty as a cattle-like existence produced by humanity's self-destructive pursuit of perfect security.

passages.text:
“It is a law of nature we overlook, that intellectual versatility is
the compensation for change, danger, and trouble. An animal perfectly
in harmony with its environment is a perfect mechanism. Nature never
appeals to intelligence until habit and instinct are useless. There is
no intelligence where there is no change and no need of change. Only
those animals partake of intelligence that have to meet a huge variety
of needs and dangers.

“So, as I see it, the Upperworld man had drifted towards his feeble
prettiness, and the Underworld to mere mechanical industry. But that
perfect state had lacked one thing even for mechanical
perfection—absolute permanency. Apparently as time went on, the feeding
of an Underworld, however it was effected, had become disjointed.
Mother Necessity, who had been staved off for a few thousand years,
came back again, and she began below. The Underworld being in contact
with machinery, which, however perfect, still needs some little thought
outside habit, had probably retained perforce rather more initiative,
if less of every other human character, than the Upper. And when other
meat failed them, they turned to what old habit had hitherto forbidden.
So I say I saw it in my last view of the world of Eight Hundred and Two
Thousand Seven Hundred and One. It may be as wrong an explanation as
mortal wit could invent. It is how the thing shaped itself to me, and
as that I give it to you.

“After the fatigues, excitements, and terrors of the past days, and in
spite of my grief, this seat and the tranquil view and the warm
sunlight were very pleasant. I was very tired and sleepy, and soon my
theorising passed into dozing. Catching myself at that, I took my own
hint, and spreading myself out upon the turf I had a long and
refreshing sleep.
passages.gist: The Traveller theorizes that perfect security destroyed intelligence, leaving the Upperworld feeble and the Underworld mechanical until food failure drove the latter to eat the former, then he falls asleep in the sun.

passages.text:
“I awoke a little before sunsetting. I now felt safe against being
caught napping by the Morlocks, and, stretching myself, I came on down
the hill towards the White Sphinx. I had my crowbar in one hand, and
the other hand played with the matches in my pocket.

“And now came a most unexpected thing. As I approached the pedestal of
the sphinx I found the bronze valves were open. They had slid down into
grooves.

“At that I stopped short before them, hesitating to enter.

“Within was a small apartment, and on a raised place in the corner of
this was the Time Machine. I had the small levers in my pocket. So
here, after all my elaborate preparations for the siege of the White
Sphinx, was a meek surrender. I threw my iron bar away, almost sorry
not to use it.

“A sudden thought came into my head as I stooped towards the portal.
For once, at least, I grasped the mental operations of the Morlocks.
Suppressing a strong inclination to laugh, I stepped through the bronze
frame and up to the Time Machine. I was surprised to find it had been
carefully oiled and cleaned. I have suspected since that the Morlocks
had even partially taken it to pieces while trying in their dim way to
grasp its purpose.

“Now as I stood and examined it, finding a pleasure in the mere touch
of the contrivance, the thing I had expected happened. The bronze
panels suddenly slid up and struck the frame with a clang. I was in the
dark—trapped. So the Morlocks thought. At that I chuckled gleefully.

“I could already hear their murmuring laughter as they came towards me.
Very calmly I tried to strike the match. I had only to fix on the
levers and depart then like a ghost. But I had overlooked one little
thing. The matches were of that abominable kind that light only on the
box.
passages.gist: The Traveller finds the Sphinx open with his Time Machine restored inside, knowingly walks into the Morlocks' trap, and is sealed in the dark with unusable matches.

passages.text:
“You may imagine how all my calm vanished. The little brutes were close
upon me. One touched me. I made a sweeping blow in the dark at them
with the levers, and began to scramble into the saddle of the machine.
Then came one hand upon me and then another. Then I had simply to fight
against their persistent fingers for my levers, and at the same time
feel for the studs over which these fitted. One, indeed, they almost
got away from me. As it slipped from my hand, I had to butt in the dark
with my head—I could hear the Morlock’s skull ring—to recover it. It
was a nearer thing than the fight in the forest, I think, this last
scramble.

“But at last the lever was fixed and pulled over. The clinging hands
slipped from me. The darkness presently fell from my eyes. I found
myself in the same grey light and tumult I have already described.

“I have already told you of the sickness and confusion that comes with
time travelling. And this time I was not seated properly in the saddle,
but sideways and in an unstable fashion. For an indefinite time I clung
to the machine as it swayed and vibrated, quite unheeding how I went,
and when I brought myself to look at the dials again I was amazed to
find where I had arrived. One dial records days, and another thousands
of days, another millions of days, and another thousands of millions.
Now, instead of reversing the levers, I had pulled them over so as to
go forward with them, and when I came to look at these indicators I
found that the thousands hand was sweeping round as fast as the seconds
hand of a watch—into futurity.

“As I drove on, a peculiar change crept over the appearance of things.
The palpitating greyness grew darker; then—though I was still
travelling with prodigious velocity—the blinking succession of day and
night, which was usually indicative of a slower pace, returned, and
grew more and more marked. This puzzled me very much at first. The
alternations of night and day grew slower and slower, and so did the
passage of the sun across the sky, until they seemed to stretch through
centuries. At last a steady twilight brooded over the earth, a twilight
only broken now and then when a comet glared across the darkling sky.
The band of light that had indicated the sun had long since
disappeared; for the sun had ceased to set—it simply rose and fell in
the west, and grew ever broader and more red. All trace of the moon had
vanished. The circling of the stars, growing slower and slower, had
given place to creeping points of light. At last, some time before I
stopped, the sun, red and very large, halted motionless upon the
horizon, a vast dome glowing with a dull heat, and now and then
suffering a momentary extinction. At one time it had for a little while
glowed more brilliantly again, but it speedily reverted to its sullen
red heat. I perceived by this slowing down of its rising and setting
that the work of the tidal drag was done. The earth had come to rest
with one face to the sun, even as in our own time the moon faces the
earth. Very cautiously, for I remembered my former headlong fall, I
began to reverse my motion. Slower and slower went the circling hands
until the thousands one seemed motionless and the daily one was no
longer a mere mist upon its scale. Still slower, until the dim outlines
of a desolate beach grew visible.
passages.gist: The Traveller fights off the Morlocks to engage his machine, is hurled far forward in time by mistake, and watches the sun swell red and halt as Earth becomes tidally locked before stopping at a desolate beach.

passages.text:
“I stopped very gently and sat upon the Time Machine, looking round.
The sky was no longer blue. North-eastward it was inky black, and out
of the blackness shone brightly and steadily the pale white stars.
Overhead it was a deep Indian red and starless, and south-eastward it
grew brighter to a glowing scarlet where, cut by the horizon, lay the
huge hull of the sun, red and motionless. The rocks about me were of a
harsh reddish colour, and all the trace of life that I could see at
first was the intensely green vegetation that covered every projecting
point on their south-eastern face. It was the same rich green that one
sees on forest moss or on the lichen in caves: plants which like these
grow in a perpetual twilight.

“The machine was standing on a sloping beach. The sea stretched away to
the south-west, to rise into a sharp bright horizon against the wan
sky. There were no breakers and no waves, for not a breath of wind was
stirring. Only a slight oily swell rose and fell like a gentle
breathing, and showed that the eternal sea was still moving and living.
And along the margin where the water sometimes broke was a thick
incrustation of salt—pink under the lurid sky. There was a sense of
oppression in my head, and I noticed that I was breathing very fast.
The sensation reminded me of my only experience of mountaineering, and
from that I judged the air to be more rarefied than it is now.

“Far away up the desolate slope I heard a harsh scream, and saw a thing
like a huge white butterfly go slanting and fluttering up into the sky
and, circling, disappear over some low hillocks beyond. The sound of
its voice was so dismal that I shivered and seated myself more firmly
upon the machine. Looking round me again, I saw that, quite near, what
I had taken to be a reddish mass of rock was moving slowly towards me.
Then I saw the thing was really a monstrous crab-like creature. Can you
imagine a crab as large as yonder table, with its many legs moving
slowly and uncertainly, its big claws swaying, its long antennæ, like
carters’ whips, waving and feeling, and its stalked eyes gleaming at
you on either side of its metallic front? Its back was corrugated and
ornamented with ungainly bosses, and a greenish incrustation blotched
it here and there. I could see the many palps of its complicated mouth
flickering and feeling as it moved.
passages.gist: The Traveller surveys a desolate far-future beach under a motionless red sun and encounters giant strange creatures.

passages.text:
“As I stared at this sinister apparition crawling towards me, I felt a
tickling on my cheek as though a fly had lighted there. I tried to
brush it away with my hand, but in a moment it returned, and almost
immediately came another by my ear. I struck at this, and caught
something threadlike. It was drawn swiftly out of my hand. With a
frightful qualm, I turned, and I saw that I had grasped the antenna of
another monster crab that stood just behind me. Its evil eyes were
wriggling on their stalks, its mouth was all alive with appetite, and
its vast ungainly claws, smeared with an algal slime, were descending
upon me. In a moment my hand was on the lever, and I had placed a month
between myself and these monsters. But I was still on the same beach,
and I saw them distinctly now as soon as I stopped. Dozens of them
seemed to be crawling here and there, in the sombre light, among the
foliated sheets of intense green.

“I cannot convey the sense of abominable desolation that hung over the
world. The red eastern sky, the northward blackness, the salt Dead Sea,
the stony beach crawling with these foul, slow-stirring monsters, the
uniform poisonous-looking green of the lichenous plants, the thin air
that hurts one’s lungs: all contributed to an appalling effect. I moved
on a hundred years, and there was the same red sun—a little larger, a
little duller—the same dying sea, the same chill air, and the same
crowd of earthy crustacea creeping in and out among the green weed and
the red rocks. And in the westward sky, I saw a curved pale line like a
vast new moon.

“So I travelled, stopping ever and again, in great strides of a
thousand years or more, drawn on by the mystery of the earth’s fate,
watching with a strange fascination the sun grow larger and duller in
the westward sky, and the life of the old earth ebb away. At last, more
than thirty million years hence, the huge red-hot dome of the sun had
come to obscure nearly a tenth part of the darkling heavens. Then I
stopped once more, for the crawling multitude of crabs had disappeared,
and the red beach, save for its livid green liverworts and lichens,
seemed lifeless. And now it was flecked with white. A bitter cold
assailed me. Rare white flakes ever and again came eddying down. To the
north-eastward, the glare of snow lay under the starlight of the sable
sky, and I could see an undulating crest of hillocks pinkish white.
There were fringes of ice along the sea margin, with drifting masses
farther out; but the main expanse of that salt ocean, all bloody under
the eternal sunset, was still unfrozen.
passages.gist: The Traveller escapes a rear crab attack with a short time jump, then travels in ever-longer strides millions of years forward as the sun swells, the crabs vanish, and freezing snow begins.

passages.text:
“I looked about me to see if any traces of animal life remained. A
certain indefinable apprehension still kept me in the saddle of the
machine. But I saw nothing moving, in earth or sky or sea. The green
slime on the rocks alone testified that life was not extinct. A shallow
sandbank had appeared in the sea and the water had receded from the
beach. I fancied I saw some black object flopping about upon this bank,
but it became motionless as I looked at it, and I judged that my eye
had been deceived, and that the black object was merely a rock. The
stars in the sky were intensely bright and seemed to me to twinkle very
little.

“Suddenly I noticed that the circular westward outline of the sun had
changed; that a concavity, a bay, had appeared in the curve. I saw this
grow larger. For a minute perhaps I stared aghast at this blackness
that was creeping over the day, and then I realised that an eclipse was
beginning. Either the moon or the planet Mercury was passing across the
sun’s disk. Naturally, at first I took it to be the moon, but there is
much to incline me to believe that what I really saw was the transit of
an inner planet passing very near to the earth.

“The darkness grew apace; a cold wind began to blow in freshening gusts
from the east, and the showering white flakes in the air increased in
number. From the edge of the sea came a ripple and whisper. Beyond
these lifeless sounds the world was silent. Silent? It would be hard to
convey the stillness of it. All the sounds of man, the bleating of
sheep, the cries of birds, the hum of insects, the stir that makes the
background of our lives—all that was over. As the darkness thickened,
the eddying flakes grew more abundant, dancing before my eyes; and the
cold of the air more intense. At last, one by one, swiftly, one after
the other, the white peaks of the distant hills vanished into
blackness. The breeze rose to a moaning wind. I saw the black central
shadow of the eclipse sweeping towards me. In another moment the pale
stars alone were visible. All else was rayless obscurity. The sky was
absolutely black.
passages.gist: The Traveller finds a motionless, nearly lifeless shore under bright stars, then watches an eclipse deepen into freezing, silent, absolute blackness.

passages.text:
“A horror of this great darkness came on me. The cold, that smote to my
marrow, and the pain I felt in breathing, overcame me. I shivered, and
a deadly nausea seized me. Then like a red-hot bow in the sky appeared
the edge of the sun. I got off the machine to recover myself. I felt
giddy and incapable of facing the return journey. As I stood sick and
confused I saw again the moving thing upon the shoal—there was no
mistake now that it was a moving thing—against the red water of the
sea. It was a round thing, the size of a football perhaps, or, it may
be, bigger, and tentacles trailed down from it; it seemed black against
the weltering blood-red water, and it was hopping fitfully about. Then
I felt I was fainting. But a terrible dread of lying helpless in that
remote and awful twilight sustained me while I clambered upon the
saddle.

“So I came back. For a long time I must have been insensible upon the
machine. The blinking succession of the days and nights was resumed,
the sun got golden again, the sky blue. I breathed with greater
freedom. The fluctuating contours of the land ebbed and flowed. The
hands spun backward upon the dials. At last I saw again the dim shadows
of houses, the evidences of decadent humanity. These, too, changed and
passed, and others came. Presently, when the million dial was at zero,
I slackened speed. I began to recognise our own pretty and familiar
architecture, the thousands hand ran back to the starting-point, the
night and day flapped slower and slower. Then the old walls of the
laboratory came round me. Very gently, now, I slowed the mechanism
down.

“I saw one little thing that seemed odd to me. I think I have told you
that when I set out, before my velocity became very high, Mrs. Watchett
had walked across the room, travelling, as it seemed to me, like a
rocket. As I returned, I passed again across that minute when she
traversed the laboratory. But now her every motion appeared to be the
exact inversion of her previous ones. The door at the lower end opened,
and she glided quietly up the laboratory, back foremost, and
disappeared behind the door by which she had previously entered. Just
before that I seemed to see Hillyer for a moment; but he passed like a
flash.
passages.gist: The Traveller endures freezing darkness, sees a hopping tentacled creature at sunrise, then rides the machine backward through time to his laboratory where familiar motions run in reverse.

passages.text:
“Then I stopped the machine, and saw about me again the old familiar
laboratory, my tools, my appliances just as I had left them. I got off
the thing very shakily, and sat down upon my bench. For several minutes
I trembled violently. Then I became calmer. Around me was my old
workshop again, exactly as it had been. I might have slept there, and
the whole thing have been a dream.

“And yet, not exactly! The thing had started from the south-east corner
of the laboratory. It had come to rest again in the north-west, against
the wall where you saw it. That gives you the exact distance from my
little lawn to the pedestal of the White Sphinx, into which the
Morlocks had carried my machine.

“For a time my brain went stagnant. Presently I got up and came through
the passage here, limping, because my heel was still painful, and
feeling sorely begrimed. I saw the _Pall Mall Gazette_ on the table by
the door. I found the date was indeed today, and looking at the
timepiece, saw the hour was almost eight o’clock. I heard your voices
and the clatter of plates. I hesitated—I felt so sick and weak. Then I
sniffed good wholesome meat, and opened the door on you. You know the
rest. I washed, and dined, and now I am telling you the story.

“I know,” he said, after a pause, “that all this will be absolutely
incredible to you, but to me the one incredible thing is that I am here
tonight in this old familiar room looking into your friendly faces and
telling you these strange adventures.” He looked at the Medical Man.
“No. I cannot expect you to believe it. Take it as a lie—or a prophecy.
Say I dreamed it in the workshop. Consider I have been speculating upon
the destinies of our race, until I have hatched this fiction. Treat my
assertion of its truth as a mere stroke of art to enhance its interest.
And taking it as a story, what do you think of it?”
passages.gist: The Traveller arrives back in his familiar workshop and dining room, cites the machine's changed position as physical proof, yet tells his listeners they may disbelieve him and judge his tale as fiction.

passages.text:
He took up his pipe, and began, in his old accustomed manner, to tap
with it nervously upon the bars of the grate. There was a momentary
stillness. Then chairs began to creak and shoes to scrape upon the
carpet. I took my eyes off the Time Traveller’s face, and looked round
at his audience. They were in the dark, and little spots of colour swam
before them. The Medical Man seemed absorbed in the contemplation of
our host. The Editor was looking hard at the end of his cigar—the
sixth. The Journalist fumbled for his watch. The others, as far as I
remember, were motionless.

The Editor stood up with a sigh. “What a pity it is you’re not a writer
of stories!” he said, putting his hand on the Time Traveller’s
shoulder.

“You don’t believe it?”

“Well——”

“I thought not.”

The Time Traveller turned to us. “Where are the matches?” he said. He
lit one and spoke over his pipe, puffing. “To tell you the truth... I
hardly believe it myself..... And yet...”

His eye fell with a mute inquiry upon the withered white flowers upon
the little table. Then he turned over the hand holding his pipe, and I
saw he was looking at some half-healed scars on his knuckles.

The Medical Man rose, came to the lamp, and examined the flowers. “The
gynæceum’s odd,” he said. The Psychologist leant forward to see,
holding out his hand for a specimen.

“I’m hanged if it isn’t a quarter to one,” said the Journalist. “How
shall we get home?”

“Plenty of cabs at the station,” said the Psychologist.

“It’s a curious thing,” said the Medical Man; “but I certainly don’t
know the natural order of these flowers. May I have them?”

The Time Traveller hesitated. Then suddenly: “Certainly not.”

“Where did you really get them?” said the Medical Man.
passages.gist: The listeners meet the tale with restless scepticism and talk of going home while the Traveller appeals to the strange flowers and his scarred knuckles and refuses to give the flowers up.

passages.text:
The Time Traveller put his hand to his head. He spoke like one who was
trying to keep hold of an idea that eluded him. “They were put into my
pocket by Weena, when I travelled into Time.” He stared round the room.
“I’m damned if it isn’t all going. This room and you and the atmosphere
of every day is too much for my memory. Did I ever make a Time Machine,
or a model of a Time Machine? Or is it all only a dream? They say life
is a dream, a precious poor dream at times—but I can’t stand another
that won’t fit. It’s madness. And where did the dream come from? … I
must look at that machine. If there is one!”

He caught up the lamp swiftly, and carried it, flaring red, through the
door into the corridor. We followed him. There in the flickering light
of the lamp was the machine sure enough, squat, ugly, and askew, a
thing of brass, ebony, ivory, and translucent glimmering quartz. Solid
to the touch—for I put out my hand and felt the rail of it—and with
brown spots and smears upon the ivory, and bits of grass and moss upon
the lower parts, and one rail bent awry.

The Time Traveller put the lamp down on the bench, and ran his hand
along the damaged rail. “It’s all right now,” he said. “The story I
told you was true. I’m sorry to have brought you out here in the cold.”
He took up the lamp, and, in an absolute silence, we returned to the
smoking-room.

He came into the hall with us and helped the Editor on with his coat.
The Medical Man looked into his face and, with a certain hesitation,
told him he was suffering from overwork, at which he laughed hugely. I
remember him standing in the open doorway, bawling good-night.
passages.gist: The Traveller briefly doubts his own story as a dream, but the solid, travel-stained machine in the corridor restores his certainty before the guests leave with a conventional explanation.

passages.text:
I shared a cab with the Editor. He thought the tale a “gaudy lie.” For
my own part I was unable to come to a conclusion. The story was so
fantastic and incredible, the telling so credible and sober. I lay
awake most of the night thinking about it. I determined to go next day
and see the Time Traveller again. I was told he was in the laboratory,
and being on easy terms in the house, I went up to him. The laboratory,
however, was empty. I stared for a minute at the Time Machine and put
out my hand and touched the lever. At that the squat
substantial-looking mass swayed like a bough shaken by the wind. Its
instability startled me extremely, and I had a queer reminiscence of
the childish days when I used to be forbidden to meddle. I came back
through the corridor. The Time Traveller met me in the smoking-room. He
was coming from the house. He had a small camera under one arm and a
knapsack under the other. He laughed when he saw me, and gave me an
elbow to shake. “I’m frightfully busy,” said he, “with that thing in
there.”

“But is it not some hoax?” I said. “Do you really travel through time?”

“Really and truly I do.” And he looked frankly into my eyes. He
hesitated. His eye wandered about the room. “I only want half an hour,”
he said. “I know why you came, and it’s awfully good of you. There’s
some magazines here. If you’ll stop to lunch I’ll prove you this time
travelling up to the hilt, specimens and all. If you’ll forgive my
leaving you now?”

I consented, hardly comprehending then the full import of his words,
and he nodded and went on down the corridor. I heard the door of the
laboratory slam, seated myself in a chair, and took up a daily paper.
What was he going to do before lunch-time? Then suddenly I was reminded
by an advertisement that I had promised to meet Richardson, the
publisher, at two. I looked at my watch, and saw that I could barely
save that engagement. I got up and went down the passage to tell the
Time Traveller.
passages.gist: The undecided narrator returns next day, finds the machine uncannily insubstantial, and leaves the Traveller equipping himself to deliver a promised proof in order to keep another engagement.

passages.text:
As I took hold of the handle of the door I heard an exclamation, oddly
truncated at the end, and a click and a thud. A gust of air whirled
round me as I opened the door, and from within came the sound of broken
glass falling on the floor. The Time Traveller was not there. I seemed
to see a ghostly, indistinct figure sitting in a whirling mass of black
and brass for a moment—a figure so transparent that the bench behind
with its sheets of drawings was absolutely distinct; but this phantasm
vanished as I rubbed my eyes. The Time Machine had gone. Save for a
subsiding stir of dust, the further end of the laboratory was empty. A
pane of the skylight had, apparently, just been blown in.

I felt an unreasonable amazement. I knew that something strange had
happened, and for the moment could not distinguish what the strange
thing might be. As I stood staring, the door into the garden opened,
and the man-servant appeared.

We looked at each other. Then ideas began to come. “Has Mr. —— gone out
that way?” said I.

“No, sir. No one has come out this way. I was expecting to find him
here.”

At that I understood. At the risk of disappointing Richardson I stayed
on, waiting for the Time Traveller; waiting for the second, perhaps
still stranger story, and the specimens and photographs he would bring
with him. But I am beginning now to fear that I must wait a lifetime.
The Time Traveller vanished three years ago. And, as everybody knows
now, he has never returned.

One cannot choose but wonder. Will he ever return? It may be that he
swept back into the past, and fell among the blood-drinking, hairy
savages of the Age of Unpolished Stone; into the abysses of the
Cretaceous Sea; or among the grotesque saurians, the huge reptilian
brutes of the Jurassic times. He may even now—if I may use the
phrase—be wandering on some plesiosaurus-haunted Oolitic coral reef, or
beside the lonely saline seas of the Triassic Age. Or did he go
forward, into one of the nearer ages, in which men are still men, but
with the riddles of our own time answered and its wearisome problems
solved? Into the manhood of the race: for I, for my own part, cannot
think that these latter days of weak experiment, fragmentary theory,
and mutual discord are indeed man’s culminating time! I say, for my own
part. He, I know—for the question had been discussed among us long
before the Time Machine was made—thought but cheerlessly of the
Advancement of Mankind, and saw in the growing pile of civilisation
only a foolish heaping that must inevitably fall back upon and destroy
its makers in the end. If that is so, it remains for us to live as
though it were not so. But to me the future is still black and blank—is
a vast ignorance, lit at a few casual places by the memory of his
story. And I have by me, for my comfort, two strange white
flowers—shrivelled now, and brown and flat and brittle—to witness that
even when mind and strength had gone, gratitude and a mutual tenderness
still lived on in the heart of man.
passages.gist: The narrator witnesses the Time Traveller's sudden vanishing in his machine, waits three fruitless years for his return, and closes with wondering speculation and tender memorial.

units.state: The machine is no longer overturned on soft turf; it now stands on a sloping beach beside a windless sea in the far future.

evidence.quote: sitting on soft turf in front of the overset machine

units.label: Hail Beaten Garden Lawn
units.content: He finds himself in a garden where rhododendron bushes shed blossoms under the hail.
units.state: The Traveller is no longer in the Hail Beaten Garden Lawn but now stands with his machine on the Sloping Salt-Edged Beach.

evidence.quote: garden, surrounded by rhododendron bushes, and I noticed that their

units.label: Colossal White Winged Statue
units.content: A huge white marble winged sphinx-like figure on a bronze pedestal looms over the garden.
units.reading: The Colossal White Winged Statue is now understood as a mocking triumphant watcher hinting at hostile intervention like the Smiling Marble Sphinx Watcher and Mocking sphinx smile, not merely a neutral looming monument.
other_readings: The bronze base beneath the looming white figure is also to be understood as a hollow container with door-like panels that can hide the machine, in addition to being a mocking watcher.

evidence.quote: A colossal figure, carved apparently in some white

units.label: Weather-Worn Diseased Omen
units.content: The statue's weather-worn condition gives an unpleasant suggestion of disease.

evidence.quote: suggestion of disease. I stood looking at it for a little space—half a

units.label: Clearing Hail Sunlight Promise
units.content: The hail curtain thins and the sky lightens with the promise of sun.
units.state: The hailstorm has now been swept aside and vanished, with sunlight breaking through.

evidence.quote: that the sky was lightening with the promise of the sun

units.label: Future humanity turned cruel
units.content: The Traveller fears future men may have become cruel, inhuman, and overwhelmingly powerful.
units.reading: Future humanity turned cruel is now to be read as no longer dismissible as misplaced because the overwhelming threat may reside in the subterranean second branch rather than the frail surface people.
other_readings: The fear that Future humanity turned cruel can no longer be dismissed as misplaced from surface frailty alone now that Humanity Split Species leaves a second underground branch still to be judged.

evidence.quote: What if cruelty had grown into a common passion?

units.label: Panicked attempt to escape
units.content: Seized by panic at the vast buildings, he frantically tries to readjust the Time Machine.

evidence.quote:
I turned
frantically to the Time Machine, and strove hard to readjust it

units.label: Storm vanishes like ghost
units.content: The grey storm downpour vanishes like a ghost's trailing garments as sunlight breaks through.

evidence.quote:
The grey
downpour was swept aside and vanished like the trailing garments of a
ghost

units.label: Naked prey vulnerability
units.content: He feels exposed and prey-like, as a bird knowing a hawk is above and will swoop.
units.state: He no longer feels exposed and prey-like; the fearless bearing of the small creature has restored his confidence.

evidence.quote:
I felt as perhaps
a bird may feel in the clear air, knowing the hawk wings above and will
swoop

units.label: First sight of watchers
units.content: With retreat secured and courage recovered, he sees robed figures watching him from high in a nearby house.
units.reading: First sight of watchers is now a first glimpse of the same frail Watching Uniform Diners peering from already worn and dilapidated houses, not powerful overseers in intact splendour.

evidence.quote:
In a circular opening, high up in the wall of the nearer house,
I saw a group of figures clad in rich soft robes

units.label: Small Men Approach
units.content: A group of running small men approaches the Traveller from the bushes by the White Sphinx.

evidence.quote: White Sphinx were the heads and shoulders of men running

units.label: Frail Future People
units.content: The future people are slight, beautiful, graceful, and indescribably frail beings.
units.reading: Frail Future People are now also to be read as enfeebled by perfect security which rewarded feebleness.
other_readings: Frail future people are now also to be read as the end-point after secure energy burned briefly in art and eroticism and then sank into languor, not only as direct enfeeblement by security.
The Frail Future People are now to be read as only the surface branch of a humanity split into two species, still frail from security but no longer the whole of humanity.
The slight beautiful frail people are now also to be understood as descendants of the Capitalist upper branch maintained by underground labour, in addition to being enfeebled by security.
The slight beautiful frail beings should now also be understood as decaying doomed prey whose former servants are creeping on as their nemesis in a reversed class order.
Frail Future People remain slight and frail and preyed upon, but are also still recognizably human whose form compels sympathy, so they cannot be regarded with detachment as mere cattle.
Slight beautiful graceful frail beings are also to be understood as living a pleasant heedless cattle-like existence ending as prey.

evidence.quote: He was a slight creature—perhaps four feet

units.label: Fearlessness Restores Confidence
units.content: The creature's complete lack of fear strikes the Traveller and restores his confidence.

evidence.quote: The absence from his bearing of any sign of fear struck me

units.label: Tactile Reality Check
units.content: The small people touch the Traveller's hands, back, and shoulders to make sure he is real.

evidence.quote: Then I felt other soft little tentacles upon my back and

units.label: Removing Machine Levers
units.content: The Traveller unscrews the starting levers from the Time Machine to keep the visitors from setting it in motion.
units.state: The starting levers are no longer removed and safekept; they have been fixed back onto the machine and pulled for escape.

evidence.quote: machine I unscrewed the little levers that would set it in motion

units.label: Delicate Future People
units.content: The future people have a delicate Dresden-china prettiness with small, childlike features and large mild eyes.
units.reading: Delicate Future People are now also to be read as the languor endpoint after secure energy burned briefly in art and eroticism, not only as directly enfeebled by security.
other_readings: The delicate Dresden-china people are only the surface branch of a humanity now split into two distinct species, still showing enfeeblement after security but no longer taken as the whole of humanity.
Delicate Future People are now also to be read as the Capitalist-descended surface branch maintained by hidden underground labour while remaining the languor endpoint.
The Delicate Future People are now also to be understood as decaying doomed prey whose former servants are creeping on as their nemesis.
Delicate Future People remain delicate Dresden-china pretty beings but are also still recognizably human whose form compels sympathy so they cannot be regarded with detachment as mere cattle.
Delicate Future People are also to be understood as living a pleasant heedless cattle-like existence ending as prey.

evidence.quote: peculiarities in their Dresden china type of prettiness

units.label: Passive Cooing Onlookers
units.content: The future people surround the Traveller smiling and cooing to each other without attempting to communicate with him.

evidence.quote:
but simply stood round
me smiling and speaking in soft cooing notes to each other

units.label: Sun Gesture Thunder Mimicry
units.content: When the Traveller points to the sun, a little figure copies the gesture and astonishes him by imitating thunder.

evidence.quote:
followed my gesture, and then astonished me by imitating the sound of
thunder

units.label: Expected Future Superiority
units.content: The Traveller had always expected the people of 802,000 to be vastly ahead in knowledge, art, and everything.
units.reading: Expected Future Superiority should now be understood as a naive absurd assumption about inevitable progress, not as a reasonable forecast.

evidence.quote:
would be incredibly in front of us in knowledge, art,
everything

units.label: Childlike Sun Thunder Question
units.content: One of the creatures asks if the Traveller came from the sun in a thunderstorm, showing five-year-old intellect.
units.reading: Childlike Sun Thunder Question is now also to be read as illustration that Victorian restless energy become weakness left only childlike intellect.

evidence.quote:
asked me, in fact, if I had come from the sun in a
thunderstorm!

units.label: Time Machine Built Vain
units.content: The Traveller is flooded with disappointment and feels for a moment that he built the Time Machine in vain.
units.reading: Time Machine Built Vain should now be understood as disappointment caused by the collapse of Expected Future Superiority now exposed as Absurd future progress assumption.

evidence.quote:
For a moment I felt that I had
built the Time Machine in vain

units.label: Thunderclap Mime Startles Crowd
units.content: The Traveller mimes a thunderclap and the little people withdraw and bow.

evidence.quote: a thunderclap as startled them. They all withdrew a pace or so and

units.label: Flower Garland Smothering
units.content: The crowd laughingly runs for flowers and piles blossoms on the Traveller.

evidence.quote: to and fro for flowers, and laughingly flinging them upon me until I

units.label: Smiling Marble Sphinx Watcher
units.content: A white marble sphinx seems to watch the Traveller with a smile at his astonishment.
units.reading: The watching smile should now be understood as mocking triumph hinting at hostile intervention, not merely curious watching at astonishment.

evidence.quote: which had seemed to watch me all the while with a

units.label: Mocked Intellectual Posterity Hope
units.content: The Traveller recalls his confident expectation of a grave intellectual posterity with irresistible merriment.

evidence.quote: profoundly grave and intellectual posterity came, with irresistible

units.label: Weedless Neglected Future Garden
units.content: The world beyond the crowd is a long-neglected yet weedless tangle of beautiful bushes and flowers.
units.reading: Weedless Neglected Future Garden is now also to be read as subjugated nature staying weedless combined with neglect from enfeebled maintainers.

evidence.quote: was a tangled waste of beautiful bushes and flowers, a long

units.label: Vast Brown-Hung Hall
units.content: The big doorway opens into a huge hall hung with brown and lit by tempered coloured-glass light.

evidence.quote: The big doorway opened into a proportionately great hall hung with

units.content: The hall floor of huge hard white-metal blocks is deeply channelled by the traffic of past generations.

evidence.quote:
it was so much worn, as I judged by the
going to and fro of past generations, as to be deeply channelled along

units.label: Hand-Eaten Fruit Meal
units.content: The conductors and Traveller sit on cushions and eat fruit by hand, tossing peel and stalks into table openings.

evidence.quote:
they began to eat the fruit with
their hands, flinging peel and stalks, and so forth, into the round

units.label: Dilapidated Look Strikes
units.content: The hall's dilapidated look is what strikes the narrator most.

evidence.quote: perhaps the thing that struck me most was its dilapidated look

units.label: Watching Uniform Diners
units.content: About two hundred identical soft silky-clad diners crowd near and watch the Traveller with shining little eyes.

evidence.quote:
most of them, seated as near to
me as they could come, were watching me with interest, their little
eyes shining over the fruit they were eating. All were clad in the same
soft, and yet strong, silky material

units.label: All-fruit vegetarian diet
units.content: The remote future people live entirely on fruit, forcing the narrator to become frugivorous too.

evidence.quote: Fruit, by the bye, was all their diet

units.label: Domestic animals extinct
units.content: Common domestic animals have died out in this future world.

evidence.quote: afterwards that horses, cattle, sheep, dogs, had followed the

units.label: Floury husk staple fruit
units.content: A floury fruit in a three-sided husk becomes the narrator's staple food.

evidence.quote: a floury thing in a three-sided husk—was especially good

units.label: Learning language from fruit
units.content: The narrator starts learning their speech by holding up fruits and using interrogative sounds and gestures.

evidence.quote: holding one of these up I began a series of

units.label: Indolent easily fatigued people
units.content: The little people are extremely indolent and easily fatigued by his interrogations.

evidence.quote: people more indolent or more easily fatigued

units.label: Hosts' Fleeting Curiosity
units.content: The little hosts approach with eager astonishment but soon wander away like children.

evidence.quote: their lack of interest. They would come to me with eager cries of

units.label: Traveller Disregards Hosts
units.content: The Traveller speedily comes to disregard the little people.
units.state: He no longer disregards the little people but cherishes Weena's clinging fondness, watches for her, and feels returning to the White Sphinx neighbourhood almost like coming home.

evidence.quote: speedily I came to disregard these little people

units.label: Machine's Far Future Date
units.content: The machine's dials record the date as A.D. 802,701.
units.state: The dials no longer stand at 802,701; they are spinning rapidly onward into far deeper futurity.

evidence.quote: Hundred and Two Thousand Seven Hundred and One, A.D

units.label: Ruinous Splendour Condition
units.content: The future world exists in a confusing condition of ruinous splendour.
units.reading: The condition of ruinous splendour is now to be understood as the aftermath of the civilising climax, where complete security removed need and left splendour without vigour to maintain it.
other_readings: The condition of ruinous splendour is now to be read as proof of perfect conquest: vast grandeur as what conquest built and ruin as what contented inactivity then allowed.

evidence.quote: help to explain the condition of ruinous splendour in which I found the

units.label: Granite Aluminium Ruin
units.content: A great heap of granite bound with aluminium forms a vast derelict remnant.
units.reading: Granite Aluminium Ruin is now also to be read as splendour left derelict because security removed need and vigour to maintain it.
other_readings: Granite Aluminium Ruin is now also to be read as grandeur built by perfect conquest then left derelict after secure energy passed through art into languor.

evidence.quote: great heap of granite, bound together by masses of aluminium, a vast

units.label: Promised Strange Experience
units.content: The narrator is destined to have a strange experience at that ruin to be told later.

evidence.quote: destined, at a later date, to have a very strange experience—the first

units.label: Vanished Small Houses
units.content: Small houses, cottages and separate households have vanished, leaving only palace-like buildings among greenery.

evidence.quote: there were no small houses to be seen

units.label: Communist Diagnosis
units.content: The Traveller immediately interprets the absence of private houses as communism.

evidence.quote: Communism,’ said I to myself

units.label: Uniform Sexless Appearance
units.content: The people of the future share the same costume, hairless visage, and girlish limb form with no visible sex differences.

evidence.quote:
all had the same form of costume, the same soft hairless
visage, and the same girlish rotundity of limb

units.label: Precocious Miniature Children
units.content: The Traveller judges the future children to be extremely precocious physically, as miniatures of their parents.

evidence.quote:
I judged
then that the children of that time were extremely precocious

units.label: Obsolete Family Necessities
units.content: Family, sex specialization, and occupational differentiation were only militant necessities of an age of force, now unnecessary under balanced, secure abundance.

evidence.quote:
the
institution of the family, and the differentiation of occupations are
mere militant necessities of an age

units.label: Inadequate Early Speculation
units.content: The Traveller warns that this explanation was only speculation at the time and fell far short of reality.

evidence.quote:
Later, I was to appreciate
how far it fell short of the reality

units.label: Well Under Cupola
units.content: A small cupola-covered well-like structure briefly strikes the Traveller as odd.
units.reading: The odd cupola-covered well-like structure is now to be understood as one instance of many bronze-rimmed ventilation shafts belonging to an extensive subterranean system, not an isolated oddity.
other_readings: The cupola-covered well is an inhabited access shaft with a ladder used by the pale creatures to move between surface and below, not only a ventilation shaft.

The cupola-covered well should now be read as one node in a unified puzzle connecting wells, ventilating towers, ghostly appearances, bronze gates and the missing machine, not only as a ventilation shaft.

evidence.quote: pretty little structure, like a well under a cupola

units.label: Solitary Climb to Crest
units.content: Left alone for the first time, the Traveller pushes to the crest with a strange sense of freedom and adventure.

evidence.quote: strange sense of freedom and adventure I pushed on up to the crest

units.label: Yellow Metal Seat
units.content: On the crest sits an unrecognized yellow-metal seat with griffin-head arm-rests where the Traveller rests.

evidence.quote: There I found a seat of some yellow metal that I did not recognise

units.label: Sunset Thames Panorama
units.content: Below lies the Thames valley at sunset with the river gleaming like burnished steel among palaces and greenery.
units.reading: The Thames valley sunset is now also to be read as a figure for mankind's own sunset, in addition to remaining a scenic panorama.

evidence.quote: river lay like a band of burnished steel

units.label: Earth Become Garden
units.content: The whole earth has become a garden with no hedges, property marks, or agriculture.
units.reading: Earth Become Garden is now also to be read as subjugated nature left untended after need and vigour faded.

evidence.quote: of proprietary rights, no evidences of agriculture

units.label: Partial Interpretation Warning
units.content: The Traveller warns that the evening interpretation he is about to give is only a half-truth.

evidence.quote: only a glimpse of one facet of the truth

units.label: Humanity Upon the Wane
units.content: The Traveller perceives the future humanity he has found as declining toward its end.
units.reading: Humanity upon the wane is now to be understood as differentiation into two distinct species, not simple decline of a single humanity.
other_readings: Humanity upon the wane should now also be understood as total erasure where all human activity and memory have been swept out of existence, leaving only frail creatures.

evidence.quote: It seemed to me that I had happened upon humanity upon the wane

units.label: Sunset of Mankind
units.content: The ruddy sunset becomes a figure for mankind's own decline.

evidence.quote: ruddy sunset set me thinking of the sunset of mankind

units.label: Security Rewards Feebleness
units.content: Strength comes from need, so perfect security rewards feebleness.

evidence.quote:
Strength is the outcome of need; security
sets a premium on feebleness

units.label: Civilising Amelioration Climax
units.content: The true civilising process progressively makes life more secure until reaching a climax.
units.reading: The civilising climax is now to be understood as passed, with balanced civilisation past its zenith and sunk into degeneration.

evidence.quote:
The work of ameliorating the conditions
of life—the true civilising process that makes life more and more
secure—had gone steadily on to a climax

units.label: Future Subjugation of Nature
units.content: A future intelligent, cooperative world will deliberately reshape animal and plant life to suit human needs.
units.reading: Future Subjugation of Nature is now to be read as a mistaken cooperative ideal exposed as Aristocratic Triumph Over Fellow-Man rather than a future moral reshaping of life.

evidence.quote:
In the
end, wisely and carefully we shall readjust the balance of animal and
vegetable life to suit our human needs

units.label: Cleansed Disease-Free Nature
units.content: The future natural world is cleansed of pests, weeds, fungi, and disease.

evidence.quote: The air was free from gnats, the earth from weeds or fungi

units.label: Toilless Social Paradise
units.content: Future mankind lives in splendid shelter and clothing with no toil, struggle, or commerce.
units.reading: Toilless Social Paradise is now also to be read as the perfect security that made strength useless and sent surplus energy through brief art into languor.

evidence.quote:
There were no signs of struggle, neither social nor
economical struggle

units.label: Population Growth Halted
units.content: The Traveller guesses the future solved overpopulation so numbers ceased to increase.

evidence.quote:
The difficulty of increasing population had been met,
I guessed, and population had ceased to increase

units.label: Hardship Builds Intelligence
units.content: Human intelligence and vigour are produced by hardship and freedom rewarding the strong and capable.

evidence.quote:
conditions under which the active, strong, and subtle survive and the
weaker go to the wall

units.label: Passions as Savage Survivals
units.content: Family jealousy, maternity, and passion lose justification without danger and become uncomfortable savage discords.

evidence.quote:
against connubial
jealousy, against fierce maternity, against passion of all sorts

units.label: Perfect Conquest of Nature
units.content: The Traveller interprets frail people and vast ruins as proof of humanity's perfect conquest of nature.
units.reading: Perfect Conquest of Nature should now be read as a daylight-only illusion undermined by persisting dread beyond daylight.
other_readings: Perfect Conquest of Nature is now also to be read as a daylight illusion sustained by hidden underground labour for the Capitalist-descended surface branch rather than true conquest.
Perfect conquest should now also be read as an aristocratic domination carrying the present industrial system to its conclusion, not a moral or cooperative triumph over nature.

evidence.quote: belief in a perfect conquest of Nature

units.label: Strength Becomes Weakness
units.content: Under perfect comfort and security, the restless energy that is strength for Victorians would become weakness.

evidence.quote: restless energy, that with us is strength, would become weakness

units.label: World Without Danger or Toil
units.content: After countless years without war, beasts, disease, or toil, the weak are as well equipped as the strong.

evidence.quote: what we should call the weak are as well equipped as the strong, are

units.label: Energy Decays Through Art
units.content: Secure energy inevitably turns to art and eroticism, then to languor and decay.

evidence.quote: eroticism, and then come languor and decay

units.label: Broken Grindstone of Necessity
units.content: Pain and necessity are a grindstone that kept humans keen, and here that hateful grindstone is finally broken.
units.state: Pain and necessity are no longer finally broken everywhere; after thousands of years necessity has returned below.

evidence.quote: that hateful grindstone broken at last!

units.label: Mastered World Problem
units.content: The Traveller believes his simple explanation has mastered the whole secret of the future people.
units.reading: The confident claim to have mastered the whole secret is now to be understood as mistaken overconfidence in an obvious sanitary interpretation that is retracted as absolutely wrong.

evidence.quote: explanation I had mastered the problem of the world—mastered the whole

units.label: Over-successful Population Checks
units.content: The Traveller theorizes that population checks succeeded too well and numbers declined, explaining the ruins.

evidence.quote: for the increase of population had succeeded too well, and their

units.label: Gibbous Moon Rising
units.content: A yellow gibbous moon rises in silver light as night falls and the little people disappear.
units.reading: Gibbous Moon Rising should now be read as the nightly onset of fearful hours confirmed by dawn apparitions rather than mere picturesque nightfall.
units.state: The moon is no longer gibbous and bright; it is waning toward its last quarter with nights growing dark.

evidence.quote: moon, yellow and gibbous, came up out of an overflow of silver light in

units.label: Time Machine Vanished
units.content: The Traveller realizes with shock that the Time Machine is gone from the lawn by the Sphinx.
units.state: The Time Machine is no longer missing from the lawn but is recovered waiting inside the Sphinx.

evidence.quote: The Time Machine was gone!

units.label: Fear of Stranded Helplessness
units.content: The Traveller is gripped by the physical dread of losing his own age and being left helpless.

evidence.quote: my own age, of being left helpless in this strange new world

units.label: Frantic Downhill Run
units.content: In a passion of fear the Traveller runs with leaping strides down the slope toward the lawn.

evidence.quote: passion of fear and running with great leaping strides down the slope

units.label: Empty space confrontation
units.content: The Traveller confronts the empty space where the Time Machine stood and feels faint and cold.

evidence.quote: I felt faint and cold when I faced the empty

units.label: Mocking sphinx smile
units.content: The moonlit sphinx appears to smile in mockery of the Traveller's dismay.

evidence.quote: It seemed to smile in mockery of my dismay

units.label: Unsuspected intervening power
units.content: The Traveller is dismayed by the sense that some unknown power intervened to make his invention vanish.

evidence.quote: sense of some hitherto unsuspected power, through whose intervention my

units.label: Hidden only in space
units.content: The Traveller concludes the machine was not moved in time but only hidden in space.

evidence.quote: It had moved, and was hid, only in space

units.label: Bloody bush beating
units.content: In frenzy the Traveller beats the bushes until his knuckles are gashed and bleeding.

evidence.quote: fist until my knuckles were gashed and bleeding from the broken twigs

units.label: Dark deserted hall
units.content: The great stone building's big hall is dark, silent, and deserted when the Traveller enters.

evidence.quote: The big hall was dark, silent, and deserted

units.label: Cushioned sleeping hall
units.content: The Traveller finds a second cushioned hall where many little people are sleeping.
units.reading: The cushioned hall of sleepers should now be understood not as casual rest but as the fear-driven nightly huddle against darkness.

evidence.quote: There I found a second great hall covered with cushions, upon which

units.content: The Traveller bawls for his Time Machine while seizing and shaking the little people.

evidence.quote:
Where is my
Time Machine?’ I began, bawling like an angry child, laying hands upon

units.label: Fear forgotten belief
units.content: The Traveller believes fear has been forgotten in these people based on their daylight behavior.
units.reading: The belief that fear is forgotten should now be read as true only of daylight behaviour; dawn apparitions and lingering foreboding show dread persists beyond daylight.

evidence.quote:
reasoning from their daylight behaviour, I thought that fear must be
forgotten

units.label: Nightlong maddened raving
units.content: Maddened by his loss, the Traveller raves to and fro screaming upon God and Fate.

evidence.quote:
I must have raved to and fro,
screaming and crying upon God and Fate

units.label: Sleep to morning sparrows
units.content: After utter misery the Traveller sleeps outside and wakes in full day with sparrows nearby.

evidence.quote:
Then I slept, and when I woke again it was
full day, and a couple of sparrows were hopping round me on the turf

units.label: Morning Calm Recovery
units.content: The Traveller wakes in morning freshness able to face his circumstances rationally after overnight frenzy.

evidence.quote: I sat up in the freshness of the morning, trying to remember how I had

units.label: Calm Patient Resolve
units.content: He resolves to be calm and patient to learn the people and recover or eventually remake the machine.

evidence.quote: It behoves me to be calm and patient, to learn

units.label: Failed Questioning Attempt
units.content: His attempts to question the little people fail, meeting incomprehension and mocking laughter.

evidence.quote: some thought it was a jest and laughed at me

units.label: Groove Discovery Clue
units.content: He discovers a groove ripped in the turf pointing from his arrival marks toward the sphinx pedestal.

evidence.quote: The turf gave better counsel. I found a groove ripped

units.label: Hollow Bronze Pedestal
units.content: The bronze sphinx pedestal is hollow with framed panels that look like doors opening from within.
units.reading: The hollow pedestal is also to be read as a forbidden object whose opening provokes horror and insult, in addition to being a hollow container with door-like panels.
units.state: The bronze pedestal is now slammed shut with the Traveller sealed in darkness inside.

evidence.quote: I went and rapped at these. The pedestal was hollow

units.label: Machine Inside Pedestal
units.content: He infers that his Time Machine is inside that pedestal, though how it got there is still unknown.

evidence.quote: Time Machine was inside that pedestal

units.label: Eloi Horror at Request
units.content: The Eloi treat the Traveller's gesture toward opening the pedestal as a gross insult and withdraw.

evidence.quote: They went off as if they had received the last possible insult

units.label: Seizing Eloi Guide
units.content: The Traveller angrily seizes an Eloi by the robe to drag him to the sphinx but releases him on seeing horror.

evidence.quote:
In three
strides I was after him, had him by the loose part of his robe round
the neck, and began dragging him towards the sphinx

units.label: Hammering Bronze Pedestal
units.content: The Traveller batters the bronze panels with a river pebble, flattening decoration and scattering verdigris without opening it.

evidence.quote:
Then I got
a big pebble from the river, and came and hammered till I had flattened

flakes

units.label: Chuckle Inside Pedestal
units.content: The Traveller thinks he hears a chuckle stirring inside the pedestal but dismisses it as mistaken.
units.reading: The chuckle stirring inside the pedestal should now be understood as real Morlock mocking laughter, not a mistake, anticipating the mocking pursuit in the dark.

evidence.quote:
I thought I
heard a sound like a chuckle—but I must have been mistaken

units.label: Furtive Eloi Onlookers
units.content: A crowd of Eloi watches the hammering from the slopes at a distance without intervening.

evidence.quote:
I
saw a crowd of them upon the slopes, looking furtively at me

units.label: Occidental Restless Temperament
units.content: The Traveller claims he can work for years but cannot endure inactive waiting.

evidence.quote:
I could work at a
problem for years, but to wait inactive for twenty-four hours—that is
another matter

units.label: Resolve to leave sphinx
units.content: The Traveller tells himself that patience and leaving the sphinx alone is the only way to recover his machine.

evidence.quote:
If you want your
machine again you must leave that sphinx alone

units.label: Self-made hopeless trap
units.content: The Traveller sees the humor in having trapped himself in the future after years of work to reach it.

evidence.quote:
I had made myself the most complicated and
the most hopeless trap that ever a man devised

units.label: Eloi avoidance after hammering
units.content: The little people seem to avoid the Traveller, possibly because of his hammering at the bronze gates.

evidence.quote:
it seemed to me that the little people
avoided me

units.label: Excessively simple Eloi language
units.content: The Eloi language appears excessively simple, built almost only from concrete nouns, verbs, and two-word sentences.

evidence.quote:
if
I could enter those doors and carry a blaze of light before me I should
discover the Time Machine and escape

Weena I had resolved to bring
with me to our own time

I found the Palace of Green Porcelain, when we approached it about
noon, deserted and falling into ruin

to see a large estuary, or even creek, where I judged
Wandsworth and Battersea must once have been

the bare idea of writing
had never entered her head

Further in the gallery was the huge skeleton
barrel of a Brontosaurus

units.label: Future South Kensington
units.content: The Traveller concludes the ruins are a latter-day South Kensington palaeontological collection.

evidence.quote: Clearly we stood among the ruins of some latter-day South Kensington!

units.content: Decay continues extremely slowly after the extinction of bacteria and fungi removed most of its force.

evidence.quote: extinction of bacteria and fungi, lost ninety-nine hundredths of its

evidence.quote: and very quietly took my hand and stood beside

units.content: The Traveller hopes the palace contains historical galleries or even a library.

evidence.quote:
possibly
historical galleries; it might be, even a library!

evidence.quote:
the sight of a block of sulphur set my mind
running on gunpowder

evidence.quote:
A few shrivelled and blackened vestiges of what had once
been stuffed animals

units.content: A vast dim gallery holds huge, mostly corroded and broken machines on both sides.

evidence.quote:
rising on either side of me were the huge bulks of big
machines, all greatly corroded and many broken down

units.label: Machines Against Morlocks
units.content: The Traveller hopes understanding the machines will give him powers useful against the Morlocks.

evidence.quote:
I should find myself in possession of powers that might be of
use against the Morlocks

units.label: Darkening Sloped Gallery
units.content: The gallery slopes downward until daylight narrows and ends in thick darkness.

evidence.quote:
the gallery ran down at last into a
thick darkness

units.content: Weena suddenly presses close to the Traveller, her growing apprehension alerting him to the fading light.

evidence.quote: Suddenly Weena came very close to my side

units.label: Morlock Footprints In Dust
units.content: The Traveller spots small narrow footprints breaking the dust toward the dim end of the gallery.

evidence.quote:
it appeared to be broken by a number of small
narrow footprints

units.label: Pattering From Dark Depths
units.content: The Traveller hears peculiar pattering and well-like noises coming from the remote blackness.

evidence.quote:
down in the remote blackness of
the gallery I heard a peculiar pattering

units.content: The Traveller snaps a lever from a machine to make a mace sufficient for a Morlock skull.

evidence.quote:
it snapped after a minute’s strain, and
I rejoined her with a mace in my hand

units.content: The Traveller confesses he longed to kill Morlocks despite their being his own descendants.

evidence.quote:
And I longed very much to kill
a Morlock or so

units.content: The Traveller leaves the gallery holding his mace in one hand and Weena in the other.

gallery and into another and still larger one, which at the first
glance reminded me of a military chapel hung with tattered flags

was the enormous waste of labour to
which this sombre wilderness of rotting paper testified

And at last, in one of the really air-tight cases, I found a box of
matches

to Weena’s huge delight, I solemnly performed a kind of
composite dance, whistling _The Land of the Leal_ as cheerfully as I

I
hoped to find my bar of iron not altogether inadequate for the work

I was determined to reach the White Sphinx early the next

I had been
without sleep for a night and two days, and I was feverish and

among the black bushes behind us, and dim against

evidence.quote:
I would
amaze our friends behind by lighting it

units.content: Flame is vanishingly rare without humans in a temperate climate.

evidence.quote:
what a rare thing flame must be
in the absence of man and in a temperate climate

units.label: Fire-making forgotten art
units.content: In this future decadence humanity has forgotten the art of making fire.

In this decadence, too, the art of
fire-making had been forgotten on the earth

units.label: Weena drawn to flame
units.content: Weena finds the flames wholly new and wants to run to and play with them.

evidence.quote: She wanted to run to it and play with it

units.label: Set fire spreading uphill
units.content: The Traveller's heap ignites adjacent bushes into a line of fire creeping uphill.

evidence.quote:
a curved line of fire was
creeping up the grass of the hill

units.label: Armed flight into darkness
units.content: The Traveller plunges into the black wood carrying Weena on one arm and his iron bar in the other.

evidence.quote:
Upon my left arm I carried my little one, in my right hand I had my
iron bar

units.content: Pursuing Morlocks close in and seize at the Traveller's coat and arm while Weena freezes.

evidence.quote:
I felt a tug at
my coat, then something at my arm

as I fumbled with my pocket, a struggle began in the darkness
about my knees

units.content: Lighting a match reveals the white backs of Morlocks fleeing among the trees.

evidence.quote:
I held it flaring, and saw the white backs of the Morlocks
in flight amid the trees

She was lying clutching my feet and quite
motionless, with her face to the ground

units.content: Turning about during the struggle leaves the Traveller with no idea which way his path lies.

evidence.quote:
now I had not the faintest idea in what direction lay my
path

units.content: He decides to build a fire and encamp where they are.

evidence.quote: I determined to build a fire and encamp where we were

units.label: Carbuncle Morlock Eyes
units.content: Morlock eyes shine like carbuncles out of the surrounding darkness.

evidence.quote:
Here and there out of the darkness round me the Morlocks’ eyes
shone like carbuncles

units.state: The fire made in Building smoky bonfire is no longer a controlled choking campfire but part of the raging forest fire advancing through the trees.

evidence.quote:
Very soon I had a choking smoky fire of green wood and
dry sticks, and could economise my camphor

units.label: Weena lying lifeless
units.content: Weena lies beside the iron mace like one dead and cannot be revived.

evidence.quote:
I tried what I could to revive her, but
she lay like one dead

units.content: The Traveller nods off and wakes in darkness to find the Morlocks already holding him.

evidence.quote:
I seemed just to nod and
open my eyes. But all was dark, and the Morlocks had their hands upon
me

units.content: The Traveller discovers his match-box is gone while Morlocks cling to him.

evidence.quote:
Flinging off their clinging fingers I hastily felt in my pocket for
the match-box, and—it had gone!

units.label: Monstrous spider web horror
units.content: Being heaped upon in darkness feels like being caught in a monstrous spider's web.

evidence.quote:
I felt
as if I was in a monstrous spider’s web

units.label: Counterattack with iron lever
units.content: The Traveller finds his iron lever while down and uses it to fight free.

evidence.quote:
I rolled over, and as I
did so my hand came against my iron lever

units.content: The Traveller braces with his back to a tree, resolved to make the Morlocks pay despite believing he and Weena are lost.

evidence.quote:
I knew that both I and Weena were lost, but I determined
to make the Morlocks pay for their meat

that the others were running,
in an incessant stream, as it seemed, from behind me

I saw, through the
black pillars of the nearer trees, the flames of the burning forest

With that I looked for Weena, but
she was gone

looking for some trace of Weena. But Weena was
gone

a Morlock came
blundering towards me, and past me, and went on straight into the fire!

units.label: Fire-Ringed Bright Clearing

evidence.quote:
This whole space was as bright as
day with the reflection of the fire

units.label: Dazzled Morlock Crowd

evidence.quote:
struck furiously at
them with my bar, in a frenzy of fear

units.label: Morlocks Helpless in Glare
units.content: The Morlocks are absolutely helpless and miserable in the glare, so he strikes no more of them.

evidence.quote:
I was assured of their absolute helplessness and misery in
the glare, and I struck no more of them

evidence.quote: For the most part of that night I was persuaded it was a nightmare

units.content: Three suffering Morlocks put their heads down and rush into the flames as daylight approaches.

evidence.quote:
Thrice I saw Morlocks put their heads

I tied some grass about my feet and limped on across

But that morning it left me
absolutely lonely again—terribly alone

About eight or nine in the morning I came to the same seat of yellow

Some were bathing in exactly the place where I
had saved Weena

like blots upon the landscape rose the cupolas above the ways to the

evidence.quote:
Very pleasant was their day, as pleasant as the day of
the cattle in the field

evidence.quote:
It had set itself steadfastly towards
comfort and ease, a balanced society with security and permanency as

evidence.quote: It is a law of nature we overlook, that intellectual versatility is

evidence.quote: the Upperworld man had drifted towards his feeble

evidence.quote: Mother Necessity, who had been staved off for a few thousand years

units.content: When other meat failed, the Underworld turned to food that old habit had hitherto forbidden.

units.label: Traveller Falls Asleep
units.content: Exhausted by fatigue and terror, the Traveller spreads himself on the turf for a long refreshing sleep.

evidence.quote:
spreading myself out upon the turf I had a long and
refreshing sleep
